_readme: Provenance manifest. STANDING RULE: every factual claim we publish must trace to a PRIMARY source and be citable. Where no primary source exists, the claim must be TRIANGULATED across at least two independent sources, both recorded here. Anything else is tier 'editorial', which means it is our judgement, not a fact, and must be presented as such on the page. Enforced by scripts/check_provenance.cjs. Kept as a sidecar rather than a _meta key inside each dataset, because an extra key in CITY_CLIMATE or CITY_TZ would be read as a city by every consumer.

_tiers.primary: Taken directly from the body that produces or governs the data (a met agency, IANA, a government visa portal, the photographer's licence).
_tiers.triangulated: No usable primary source, so agreed across >=2 independent secondary sources, each listed in corroboration.
_tiers.editorial: Our own judgement. Not a fact. Must be labelled as opinion wherever it is shown.

climate.source: Weather-station climate normals for 1991-2020 where a station stands for the city (WMO Climate Normals 1991-2020 via NOAA NCEI; IDEAM, Colombia's met service; Meteostat and its data providers, CC BY 4.0), Open-Meteo ERA5 reanalysis for 2019-2023 everywhere else
climate.method: Each city takes the nearest station that publishes 1991-2020 normals (mean daily high, mean daily low, monthly precipitation) when it is within 25 km of the city coordinate and within 250 m of the city's elevation; airports and WMO-indexed stations are favoured by 3 km and a national met service file beats Meteostat for the same station. Values are rounded, never adjusted for elevation or interpolated. Stations are dropped when their file coordinate disagrees with the station register or with the ground elevation, when a country's WMO submission reports extremes rather than daily means (Mongolia, Turkmenistan, Armenia, Oman, Niger), when any month fails a sanity check, and in three reviewed cases (Iloilo, Leh, one Nanaimo record). The remaining cities keep the ERA5 grid values from scripts/build_city_climate.cjs. Built by scripts/build_climate_stations.cjs; the source, station, distance and elevation difference for every city are in data/city-climate-source.json.
climate.coverage: 999 of 999 cities: 636 from a weather station (WMO 413, Meteostat 214, IDEAM 9), 363 from the ERA5 grid
climate.knownLimits: Two periods are mixed: station cities show the 1991-2020 normal, ERA5 cities the 2019-2023 average, a later and warmer window whose rain rests on five years only. ERA5 is a grid of roughly 25 km cells: against the 636 stations its annual rain was 1.12 times the measured figure at the median and off by a factor of 1.5 or more for 82 cities, mostly in mountains and on wet tropical coasts; its highs ran 0.7C cooler at the median and were more than 2C off for 79. The 363 ERA5 cities carry that margin; 18 of them are flagged in data/city-climate-source.json because the stations around them show the grid too wet or too dry. A station up to 25 km away can sit in a different microclimate (an inland airport for a coastal town has colder nights), and up to 250 m of height difference is about 1.6C.

comfort-index.source: Our comfort model, applied to the climate normals above
comfort-index.method: Each month scores 0.55 x temperature + 0.45 x rain. Temperature is 100 when the mean of the average high and low is 18-25C, minus 6 per degree outside that band and minus 5 per degree the high exceeds 30C, floored at 0. Rain is 100 up to 50mm, minus 0.5 per mm above, floored at -60. The yearly score on /comfort-index is the mean of the 12 monthly scores; a comfortable month scores 80 or more; the best months on every city guide are the three highest. The same function is copied into eight scripts and pages, which must stay identical.
comfort-index.knownLimits: The comfort band, the penalties and the 55/45 weighting are judgement, not a standard. Humidity, sunshine, wind and sea temperature are not modelled. Rain is penalised harder than cold: a dry month far below freezing keeps 45 points, a very wet month can go below zero. Inputs are station normals for 636 cities and ERA5 grid cells for 363, and the grid cities, mostly in mountains and on wet tropical coasts, carry a wider margin.

climate-source.source: The station registers and normals files named in the climate entry
climate-source.method: For every city: whether its climate normals come from a weather station or the ERA5 grid, and for a station its name, identifier (WMO index where it has one), provider, distance from the city coordinate and elevation difference. The ERA5 values a station replaced are kept beside it. Written by scripts/build_climate_stations.cjs and quoted under the weather chart of every city guide.
climate-source.coverage: 999 of 999 cities: 636 station, 363 ERA5, of which 18 flagged as doubtful against nearby stations
climate-source.knownLimits: Distances are measured from the coordinate the site stores for the city, which is a point in the centre, not the edge of the built-up area.

timezones.method: Zone resolved from each city's coordinates with tz-lookup, then evaluated at runtime by the Intl API so DST is always current.

city-airports.method: Every city is mapped to the airport a traveller would actually fly into, from the airports.csv OurAirports publishes into the public domain. Only airports with an IATA code and scheduled service are eligible: an airfield you cannot buy a ticket to is not an answer. Distance is straight-line from the city coordinate and is discounted by 60km for a large hub and 25km for a medium one, so a hub slightly further out beats a nearer regional strip, capped at 250km. Straight-line distance knows nothing about water or hard borders, so eight cities are set by hand where the nearest airport is unreachable in practice, each with its reason recorded in scripts/build_city_airports.cjs. Cities with nothing in range are recorded as unserved rather than pointed at a guess.

hero-images.method: Photographer, licence and file page recorded per image in images/cities/attribution.json and shown as a visible credit on the page. Only PD, CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA accepted.

numbeo-costs.method: Component prices scraped per city in local currency exactly as Numbeo reports them, converted to USD at apply time. Numbeo is itself crowd-sourced, so it is primary only for the Numbeo index, not for ground truth. Retrieval dates: 2026-08-05 (most cities); 2026-09-29 and 2026-10-01 (86 cities fetched directly from numbeo.com).
numbeo-costs.knownLimits: Numbeo sample sizes are small in less-visited cities and its 'last updated' date varies widely per city.

visa.source: Wikipedia 'Visa policy of X' cross-checked against official government portals
corroboration: Official e-visa and immigration portals of the destination countries (evisacuba.cu, elsalvadorpei.migracion.gob.sv, snedai.com, and equivalents)
visa.method: Default rule established from the article lead first, exceptions layered on top, then every country sanity-checked against five known passports (DE/US/UK/IN/NG) before acceptance.
visa.coverage: 15 of 117 destinations verified this way; the original 102 destinations predate this rule and their origin was never recorded
visa.knownLimits: UNVERIFIED BACKLOG: the 102 older destinations are not sourced. Mongolia's visa-free programme expires 2027-01-01 and Myanmar's visa-on-arrival entries are dated trials, so both need re-checking.

city-elevations.method: Elevation sampled at each city's stored coordinate. Not published; used by scripts/check_data_sanity.cjs to catch island and region centroids that land on high ground.

city-scores.method: 13 category scores per city. Ten are editorial judgement. Three now follow published rules: Visa Ease is one score per country from a written rubric over the entry rules for UK, US and German passports (stay on arrival, border paperwork, routes to stay longer, shared limits such as Schengen), with three documented within-country exceptions (Hong Kong, Sabah, the Aqaba zone), see docs/visa-score-rubric.md; Safety keeps each country's editorial level and orders cities inside Canada, the Nordic countries, Greenland, New Zealand and other checked countries by official police-recorded crime relative to the national rate (StatCan, Statistics Finland, SSB, BRA, Statistics Denmark, NZ Police, Eurostat NUTS3, NPA Japan, ABS, ONS, FBI), see docs/safety-score-method.md. Cost scores of cities whose monthly cost was corrected on 2026-09-29 were moved toward the score sourced cities at the same price carry. WiFi: cities with an Ookla Speedtest Global Index city median carry a score measured from it (fixed and mobile medians, August 2026); other cities are capped at one point above their country's measured score, see docs/wifi-score-method.md.
city-scores.knownLimits: Still the most visible number on the site, and ten of thirteen categories remain judgement. Safety country levels are inherited editorial values; a cross-national baseline (UNODC homicide plus Gallup safety-at-night) is drafted in docs/safety-score-cross-national-proposal.md and not applied. The safety adjustment constants (one point per doubling of the crime ratio, the 70/30 violent/property split, the caps) are judgement calls. Visa Ease reflects three reference passports only. Wifi is measured only where Ookla publishes a city median; elsewhere the measurement is a ceiling, not a value. Air quality and English remain editorial.

cost-per-month.source: Numbeo for 416 cities, our own estimate for the other 583
cost-per-month.method: Where Numbeo data exists the headline figure is reconciled against it; otherwise it is an editorial estimate. On the sourced cities it is rent for a one-bedroom in the city centre plus a one-person basket without rent, which is the TOP of the range, not a typical spend. Those cities show the range in the hero instead, described under Monthly budget range.
cost-per-month.coverage: 416 of 999 sourced, 583 estimated, each labelled on its own page
cost-per-month.knownLimits: The 583 estimated figures carry more uncertainty than the 416 sourced ones. On 2026-09-29, 24 estimates that sat outside their own page's researched range or above every Numbeo city in their country were rebuilt the way the sourced figure is built, a central rent plus a one-person Numbeo basket: rent from official statistics for Hiroshima and Kanazawa (Japan 2023 Housing and Land Survey) and Wanaka (Tenancy Services bond data), otherwise the top of the central rent range researched on the page, and the basket from the nearest Numbeo city. The working is logged per city; they stay labelled as estimates. Each city page now states which of the two it is, in a note under its Cost of Living heading; check_cost_basis.cjs is the gate. The page title and meta description still hedge with "about" rather than naming the basis, because they carry one figure and no room for the caveat. This figure is still the single number every ranking, filter and comparison sorts on, and on nine cities it describes a wider or cheaper area than a reader would live in, so those cities rank cheaper than anyone can actually manage there. Goa is the clearest and is worth stating precisely: Numbeo reports the district honestly, and the inland rents in our own guide match it, but almost every visitor lives in the Anjuna belt where rent alone exceeds the headline. Those nine pages (Amritsar added 2026-10-01) now carry a note saying what the figure covers; the ranking is unchanged, because the only substitute available is editorial rent that tested 23% off at the median.

cost-ranges.source: Numbeo cost-of-living components, converted to USD at exchangerate-api.com
cost-ranges.method: The low end is a one-bedroom outside the centre plus the one-person no-rent basket; the high end is the same basket with a one-bedroom in the centre. Rent varies, the basket is held constant, because groceries and transport do not change with the neighbourhood and Numbeo does not split them by one anyway. Built by scripts/build_cost_range.cjs, rendered by apply_cost_range.cjs, checked by check_cost_range.cjs.
cost-ranges.coverage: 412 of 999 cities. Three more (Leon, Noumea, Plymouth) are excluded because Numbeo reports rent outside the centre as higher than or equal to rent in it, which would render backwards, and Punta Cana has no rent outside the centre on Numbeo.
cost-ranges.knownLimits: The 583 estimated cities show a single estimate and no range, deliberately. They hold no cost components, so the only way to derive a second end was to read a rent range out of their own page prose. Tested against the 330 cities where the true figures are known, that method missed by 23% at the median and by more than 50% on 72 of 488 endpoints, so it was not used: a range nobody measured would look exactly like one we did. The range is also only as good as Numbeo's idea of where the city ends, and it covers rent and a basket, not flights, visas, insurance or health care.

guide-prose.source: Written from model knowledge, venue and neighbourhood names verified by search
guide-prose.method: Seven sections per city. Venue names, districts and visa mechanics were checked during writing; the price ranges and internet speeds quoted in the prose were not individually sourced.
guide-prose.coverage: 648 cities have researched long-form sections; the remainder use the older generated text
guide-prose.knownLimits: Contains specific figures (rent bands, coworking day passes, Mbps) that carry no citation.

neighborhoods.source: Written from model knowledge, district names verified by search
neighborhoods.method: 4595 entries across 999 cities. Coordinates hand-placed from known landmarks and validated against the city centre, not geocoded.
neighborhoods.coverage: 999 of 999 cities have a section, 4595 entries in total
neighborhoods.knownLimits: Coordinates are accurate to roughly a few hundred metres, fine for a map pin but not authoritative. Price levels are relative judgements.

venues.source: Google Maps ratings, mostly via aggregators that republish them, plus OpenStreetMap for location
venues.method: Venues gated at a 4.0 published rating, then geo-checked against OpenStreetMap within 25km of the city centre. 65% resolve to an OSM record, 15% carry a verified official website, 20% rest on the research pass alone. Coworking spaces may instead be admitted on confirmed current operation without a rating. Liveness re-checked 2026-10-01 (data/venue-closures.json): OpenStreetMap via Overpass for 108 cities, Nominatim for every coworking and coliving card in the rest plus a 500-card sample of cafes and stays, an HTTP fetch of every venue website, and operator location pages for chain coworking. A card is removed only on evidence of closure; scripts/check_venue_liveness.cjs keeps removed venues off the pages.
venues.coverage: 5653 venue cards across 710 cities. 138 pages quote a published rating, which is the subset the 4.0 gate and the OpenStreetMap check apply to; the rest describe a venue without claiming a score
venues.knownLimits: Most ratings came from aggregators mirroring Google rather than Google directly, because the search and scraper budgets ran out. A handful in the Sendai and Tashkent sets were conservative estimates rather than read values. The 2026-10-01 liveness check looked up 3201 of the 5657 cards directly (an OpenStreetMap or Nominatim lookup, or a fetch of the card's own website). Of all 5657, 1054 matched a live OpenStreetMap record, 1065 more have a live own website, 4 were removed as closed (The Hub by Adeva in Skopje, which closed on 30 September 2026, and three WeWork buildings the operator no longer lists: Barranquilla, Cologne Friesenplatz, Portland Pioneer Place), and 3534 could not be confirmed either way. Unconfirmed is not closed: OpenStreetMap maps few coworking spaces, the public Overpass servers stopped answering after 108 cities, and no web search was available, so most cafe and stay cards outside that sample were checked only through their website. 29 cards with a dead, parked or re-registered website are listed for review in data/venue-closures.json.

service-languages.source: Official lists first: embassy and consulate lists of providers by language, statutory registers (Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare medical register, the Styrian doctors' chamber) and city and national government open data (Seoul, Daegu, Korea Health Industry Development Institute); then the provider's own website
corroboration: Each provider's own page on its source, recorded per row as sourceUrl in data/service-languages.json
service-languages.method: Every row records the exact URL the language claim was read on and an evidence tier: official (a government or embassy list defined by working language), self-declared (the provider's own site), directory (a third-party aggregator only), or visited (we confirmed in person; unused so far). scripts/build_services.cjs refuses to build if any row lacks a sourceUrl, a known evidence tier, a known language or a real city slug. The tiers are printed on every card. scripts/verify_service_links.cjs re-fetches every url and sourceUrl and reports status, redirect target and page title, so a link that rots or starts pointing somewhere else is caught rather than assumed; the 2026-08-12 runs removed one row whose cited article did not contain the claim, dropped two invented domains, corrected a link that redirected to the wrong branch, and later dropped five more rows whose sources turned out to be a dead domain, a 404, an unreachable directory, or a site that never actually states a spoken language. The checker retries three times before calling a link dead, because a single transient failure once reported six healthy URLs as dead. One live site (vetinlisbon.pt) refuses Node's fetch entirely and was confirmed by hand.
service-languages.coverage: 70373 providers across 566 of 999 cities, 15 service types and 56 languages. 70064 official, 174 self-declared, 115 directory. Prague 7315, Bucharest 5672, Hamburg 4714, Melbourne 4396, Tokyo 3634, Buenos Aires 3375
service-languages.knownLimits: THE EVIDENCE MIX SHIFTED ON 2026-08-12. An owner decision to grow volume via aggregator directories took the directory tier from 39 rows to 105, roughly half the set, so the average row is now weaker than when the dataset was 62 rows. Many directory rows rest on a ROSTER-LEVEL claim ("the clinics we list speak English") rather than a statement about the named business; each such row says so in its note. PRIMARY FOR THE CLAIM, NOT FOR FLUENCY. We source that a provider is stated to work in a language; we have not verified that it does, and no row carries the 'visited' tier. A hospital offering interpretation is counted under the languages it interprets, which is not the same as a doctor speaking them: Chiang Mai Ram and Thonglor Pet are interpreter desks, not multilingual clinicians. The 17 directory-tier rows rest on guides and aggregators that may sell placement, making them the weakest entries. The US Consulate Chiang Mai health-facilities and legal-provider PDFs and the US Embassy Georgia mental-health resource PDF are all image-only or protected and could not be read; retrieving those would upgrade several rows and is the obvious next improvement. A Russian-language directory of Russian-speaking doctors in Georgia (needdoc.ru) is an unexploited language-defined source of the same kind. Coverage is a pilot, not a map of any city's real provision, so absence from this list means nothing. REGISTERS (2026-09-24). Japan's register is the facility's own statutory report; only Tokyo's form asks whether a language is accepted without prior consultation, so Tokyo rows require that yes while the other seven cities publish the listed language unless the facility's own note hedges it (translation device, interpreter, call first, a few words). Facilities listing more than six languages and employer clinics are refused. Korean city lists are compilations by a city or district, not statutory reports, and Seoul's pharmacy list is dated 1 January 2023. The Korea Health Industry Development Institute lists language services a hospital offers, which may be an interpreter rather than the doctor.

country-facts.method: Currency, language, mains voltage, tap water guidance, tipping norm, ride-hailing apps and emergency numbers written per country without a cited source.
country-facts.knownLimits: Emergency numbers and tap-water guidance are safety-relevant and should be moved to a primary source (ITU and each country's civil protection agency).

country-meta.method: Plug type letters per country, written without a cited source.
country-meta.knownLimits: IEC World Plugs is the obvious primary source and is not yet used.

internet-speeds.method: Median fixed-broadband and mobile download speeds read from each country page of the Global Index (the latest edition per metric, August 2026 for most), plus Ookla's own city medians where it publishes them. Stored in Mbps exactly as published and quoted rounded on the WiFi score tile of each city page that gives a speed. Metrics older than March 2026 or out of line with their own history are left out rather than filled. Extended on 2026-10-01 to every country in cities-data.js that has a Global Index page, under the same rules. Retrieval dates: 2026-09-29 (105 countries); 2026-10-01 (38 countries added).
internet-speeds.coverage: 143 countries: every country in cities-data.js for which Ookla publishes a current figure. 144 Ookla city medians, keyed by city id (Hong Kong from its own SAR market figures). 67 countries and territories in cities-data.js have no entry: 59 have no Global Index page at all, 7 have only a fixed series older than March 2026, and the Maldives has no usable figure (listed in _meta).
internet-speeds.knownLimits: National medians, not city measurements, except where a named Ookla city median is held. Speedtest results are user-initiated tests, so they lean toward people who test their connection. Ookla publishes no current mobile median for 39 of the 143 countries and no current fixed median for 2 (Eswatini, Eritrea). Small or new series (Barbados, Eritrea, Turkmenistan: two editions each) pass the same rules but carry more sampling noise.
